```{r}
#| label: setup 
#| include: false

# (1) tidyverse includes ggplot2 and lubridate, which we need for this demo 
library(tidyverse)

# (2) load data for the ggplot demos 
cancelled_raw <- read_csv("https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/479848ef-41f8-44c5-bfb5-666e0df8f574/resource/0f1cf6b1-ebf6-4928-b490-0a721cc98884/download/cancellations_by_board_august_2025.csv")

hb <- read_csv("https://www.opendata.nhs.scot/dataset/9f942fdb-e59e-44f5-b534-d6e17229cc7b/resource/652ff726-e676-4a20-abda-435b98dd7bdc/download/hb14_hb19.csv")

# (3) do some data wrangling to make the data ready for plotting 
cancelled <- cancelled_raw |>
  # Join cancelled to hb
  left_join(hb, by = join_by(HBT == HB)) |>
  # Select the variables we're interested in
  select(Month,
         HBName,
         TotalOperations,
         TotalCancelled) |>
  # Filter out/remove NA values (which were the code for a specific hospital) from HBName (SB0801 before the join) 
  filter(HBName != "NA") |>
  # Reformat the month column to separate out year, month, day using lubridate ymd()
  mutate(Month = ymd(Month, truncated = TRUE),
         Year = as.factor(year(Month))) |> 
  # Change all variable names to be snake_case
  janitor::clean_names() |> 
  # Create a total operations column by year for the bar chart  
  group_by(year) |> 
  mutate(total_operations_year = sum(total_operations)) |> 
  # ungroup the data 
  ungroup()
```

## `{ggplot2}` {.smaller}

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
* An application of Leland Wilkinson's [grammar of graphics](https://discovered.ed.ac.uk/permalink/44UOE_INST/1lk19of/alma9912442093502466) for R
* A system for iteratively and declaratively creating graphics 
* Just like grammar in a language constructs sentences, grammar of graphics constructs data visualisations 

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

![Credit: Cédric Sherer](images/ggplot2_overview.png)

:::
:::::

## Aesthetics: Inside, Outside, or both 

## {#slide21-id data-menu-title="aes inside" .scrollable}

**Within** `aes()`: the argument changes based on the values of the variable

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
#| code-line-numbers: "|4"

ggplot(data = cancelled, 
       aes(x = total_operations, 
           y = total_cancelled, 
           color = year)) + 
  geom_point() 
```


## {#slide22-id data-menu-title="aes outside" .scrollable}

**Outside** `aes()`: (): the argument is given a single value and *doesn't* change based on the values of the variable


```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
#| code-line-numbers: "|4"

ggplot(data = cancelled, 
       aes(x = total_operations, 
           y = total_cancelled)) + 
  geom_point(color = "mediumpurple")
```


## {#slide23-id data-menu-title="aes inside and outside" .scrollable}

You can specify aesthetics both inside and outside `aes()`

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
#| code-line-numbers: "|4-5"

ggplot(data = cancelled, 
       aes(x = total_cancelled,
           y = total_operations, 
           color = year)) + 
  geom_point(shape = 4)
```

[To learn more about the different aesthetic specifications](https://ggplot2.tidyverse.org/articles/ggplot2-specs.html)

## Visualising 3 variables 

* Start with a 2-variable visualisation and then add color, shape, or size 

## A note on the use of color in plots 🎨 {.smaller}

::: {.incremental}

✅color should be used with intent
🚫 not as decoration

::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
Use color to:

1. To represent values 
2. To distinguish groups
  - Particularly nominal categorical data (no intrinsic order) 
3. Emphasize information 
  - Draw attention to what matters most: a specific group, range, threshold, etc. 
  
:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

Valid cases to break these rules: 

* **Double encoding:** color repeats information already shown on an axis to reinforce information 
* **Consistency across charts:** several charts show the same groups and you want the color story to match 

:::
:::::
:::

## Visualising 3+ variables {.smaller}

Add another variable with facets!

![A sketch illustrating the difference between the two faceting systems. Source: ggplot2 (2e) book](images/facetting.png)


## Visualising 3+ variables {transition="none" .smaller} 

:::{.incremental}
::::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}

![Source: ggplot2 (2e) book](images/facetting.png)

:::

:::{.column width="50%"}

* `facet_grid()` (left) is fundamentally 2D, being made up of two independent components. 
  - `facet_grid(~row~column)` creates a matrix of panels by row & column faceting variables 
* `facet_wrap()` (right) is 1D, but wrapped into 2D to save space.
  - `facet_wrap(~variable)` makes a long ribbon of panels 

:::
:::::
:::

## Data storytelling with data visualisation {.smaller}

> Use the POP method to make your key points stand out 

:::{.incremental}
* **P = Prioritize.** Establish which data point(s) are most important. 
  - Add a headline/active title which is explanatory rather than descriptive 
  
* **O = Overstate.** Use visual emphasis like color, size contrast, annotations, etc. 
  - Adjust color, thickness, sizes. Add labels or markers to highlight key points.

* **P = Point.** Guide the audience to the focus point of your chart
  - Add annotations or graphical cues (e.g., arrows, lines, circles, boxes, etc.). 

:::

## Aesthetics: Inside, Outside, or both 

🛑 🚩 If you try and specify the color to represent the 3rd variable Year outside the `aes()` you get an error.

* For example: `geom_point(color = Year)`
* `Error: object 'Year' not found`

## Aesthetics: Inside, Outside, or both {.scrollable}

🛑 🚩 If you try and put a **single value** and not a **variable** within the `aes()` R thinks you meant it as a variable. This will not produce an error as such, but the plot will likely not be as you intended it. 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: fragment
#| code-line-numbers: "|4"

ggplot(data = cancelled, 
       aes(x = total_cancelled,
           y = total_operations, 
           color = "mediumpurple")) + 
  geom_point()
```

## `{ggplot2}` layers 

* Stacked in the order of code appearance 
* Important to keep in mind as elements written later in your code may hide or overwrite previous elements 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
#| code-line-numbers: "4-6"

cancelled |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total_operations,
             color = year))+
  geom_boxplot(whisker.linetype =  "dashed",
               box.color = "black") +
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.4) 
```

---

Layering `geom_boxplot()` over `geom_jitter()` hides the data points! 

```{r}
#| echo: true
#| output-location: slide
#| code-line-numbers: "4-6"

cancelled |>
  ggplot(aes(x = year, y = total_operations,
             color = year))+
  geom_jitter(alpha = 0.4) +
  geom_boxplot(whisker.linetype =  "dashed",
               box.color = "black") 
```

## A bit more on the faceting syntax {.smaller}

Faceting follows formula syntax (denoted with the tilda `~`)

`facet_wrap(~var1, nrow = 3)`

  * Specify the split of rows with nrow argument

`facet_grid(~var1~var2)`: var1 on x-axis (columns) and var2 on y-axis (rows)
`facet_grid(.~var1)`: var1 on x-axis (columns)

  * Dot operator optional in front of ~
  
`facet_grid(var1~.)`: var1 on y-axis (rows)
  
  * Must include dot operator after ~

You can also control the scales of your subplots with the scales argument, which takes `“free”`, `“free_x”`, or `“free_y”`. By default they are fixed
